options: Analyzing a dataset with only one row
Comparing exactly two variables
Using a single chart type for every column
Examining one variable at a time on its own
questions.explain: Univariate means one variable: its center, spread, shape, and unusual values, before relating it to other columns.

questions.q: In the illustrative data, skew() gave about 1.36 for tenure_months and about 0.18 for age. What does that tell you?
options: Tenure has a long right tail; age is close to symmetric
Age is heavily skewed and tenure is symmetric
Both columns contain missing values
Tenure has more rows than age
questions.explain: Skewness near 0 is roughly symmetric; a clearly positive value like 1.36 means a long right tail.

questions.q: The total_spend histogram shows one tall bar near zero and a couple of isolated values near 7,400 and 9,800. What should you conclude?
options: The bins are wrong and the chart should be discarded
The distribution is normal
Extreme values are stretching the axis, so investigate those rows before trusting summaries
Most customers spend about 9,800
questions.explain: A few extreme values stretch the x-axis so the rest of the distribution collapses into one bar. They deserve investigation, and mean-based summaries are unreliable until you do.

questions.q: For a right-skewed variable like total_spend (median 124.4, mean 188.1), which statement is best?
options: The mean is always the better typical value
The median is usually the better typical value because the mean is pulled toward the tail
Mean and median must be equal
Skew makes any center statistic meaningless
questions.explain: In right-skewed data the mean is dragged up by the tail. The median is more robust as a 'typical' value.

questions.q: Which pair is the most appropriate for summarizing a categorical column like region?
options: skew() and a histogram
describe() on the mean only
quantile() and a box plot
value_counts() and a bar chart (countplot)
questions.explain: Categories are counted, not averaged: value_counts() (optionally normalized) and a bar chart show how observations distribute across labels.
